extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of philosophy of science, scientists interested in methodology, and advanced readers studying induction and hypothesis testing
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying standards for assessing inductive reasoning, experimental method, hypotheses, and probabilistic inference in scientific inquiry. Geared to evaluating whether causes, experiments, and generalizations satisfy methodological criteria set out in classical treatments of induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of Causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Causes combine so that their joint action is, in general, the sum of their separate effects (the law of Composition of Causes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When two causes act together they usually produce an effect corresponding to the combined action. Apparent exceptions (e.g., when doubling a cause does not double observed effect) often arise from attending to remote rather than immediate effects; duplicating a cause often duplicates the immediate collocation even if the observable final effect does not double because a certain collocation once obtained suffices for the whole effect at that time and place. Examples: one vs two men raising a gun, one vs two sparks exploding gunpowder, single vs double doses of medicine. Doubling separated in time/place (two guns fired) does double effect. Be careful to analyze immediate vs remote effects and consider heteropathic (qualitatively different remote) outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish antecedent from means of producing antecedent
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the consequent was generated by the antecedent itself, not by the means used to produce that antecedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the means of producing an antecedent are under our control, examine whether those means could themselves have produced the consequent. Judge whether this alternative explanation is plausible by assessing our knowledge of those means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of Methods of Agreement and Difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods of Agreement and Difference are not universally applicable, particularly in complex or observational cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In pure observational contexts these methods may be of limited use; when Nature’s ‘experiment’ uses complex means we may lack analysis of those means and hence cannot identify which portion of the effects is due to the supposed cause versus unknown agencies. Natural experiments often only corroborate conclusions obtained by other methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usefulness of Method of Concomitant Variations
rubrics_metrics.description: When a cause varies alone and the effect varies correspondingly, the Method of Concomitant Variations can single out the influencing cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method can identify cause-effect links even when Agreement/Difference fail (examples: appetite increases with cold; tidal contributions of sun and moon; muscle growth during exercise). But if many influencing causes exist with none predominating, or some are continually changing, it is hard to trace the relation or assign shares to causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of experimental methods in complex combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental methods are often illusory or inconclusive when dealing with complex combinations of causes; deduction is required to disentangle complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While experiment and observation are the ultimate basis of knowledge (e.g., discovery of nerve functions), they may fail to resolve complex medical or social questions unless combined with deductive reasoning to separate interacting causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of Explanation = Limits of Induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific explanation and inductive generalization are the same, and the limits to one are the limits to the other; induction presupposes similarity among phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Induction reduces phenomena to common statements when similarity is discovered. Attempts to merge distinct phenomena under a single cause must show the cause can produce them according to the same law; otherwise the unity is merely nominal and adds no explanatory value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that a proposed unity (single cause) produce effects by the same law
rubrics_metrics.description: To legitimately generalize distinct phenomena under one cause, that cause must be shown capable of producing them according to the same law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If two forces only share a superficial attribute (e.g., both are 'attractive') but differ fundamentally in law, fusion into one explanatory law is unjustified. The cause must not merely be analogous but must account for phenomena under the same operative law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy of a hypothesis: testability by deduced consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: A hypothesis is legitimate if we can deduce consequences from it and compare those consequences with observed facts to disprove or support it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypotheses like Broussais’ localization of fevers or Gilbert’s terrestrial magnetism were justifiable because they allowed deduction of consequences to test against phenomena. Even if initially erroneous (Broussais), such hypotheses aid inquiry by making testable predictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses governed by rules of hypothesis, not induction
rubrics_metrics.description: When a theory is proposed as a hypothesis (not as a proved induction), it is governed by the rules of hypothesis: plausibility, fecundity for inquiry, and testable consequences rather than immediate inductive proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin’s theory of natural selection is an example: it was not claimed as proved by induction but as a hypothesis (a vera causa) that opened fruitful inquiry and met the criteria for legitimate hypothesis-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vera causa criterion (capability to produce similar effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: A legitimate causal hypothesis should be a 'vera causa' — a cause known or shown to be capable of producing effects of the same kind as those attributed to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation of hypotheses should include checking whether the proposed cause can, in principle and degree, produce the observed effects. The question of possibility is often one of degree; hypotheses that make plausible mechanisms and can be further tested are acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogical evidence is suggestive but not definitive
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogies between phenomena (e.g., light behaving like mechanical undulations) may justify hypotheses but do not prove identity of underlying mechanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogies can motivate hypotheses (the transmission of light resembling undulations), but one must not assume the analogous mechanism literally obtains without independent evidence. Treat analogical reasoning as a guide to plausible hypothesis, not as proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical generalizations do not presuppose causation but uniformity
rubrics_metrics.description: Early generalizations presupposed uniformity in observed phenomena, not the full causal laws; valid induction requires only uniformity within the observed class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statement 'fire burns' is grounded in observed uniformity in the class of relevant phenomena and does not imply a priori knowledge of universal causation beyond the observed scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical inference: mean vs arithmetic average; use of least squares
rubrics_metrics.description: For inductive inquiry the proper 'mean' is the most probable determination of invariable elements, which is not always the arithmetic mean; the mathematical law minimizes the sum of the squares of deviations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In cases with asymmetric deviations (many small deviations on one side, fewer large on the other), the arithmetic average may mislead; apply appropriate statistical principles (e.g., least squares) to estimate central tendencies relevant to causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability calculation requires data-grounded enumeration of possibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The calculation of chances breaks down when there are no data grounded either on special experience or special inference; listing possibilities requires empirical basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In artificial cases (colored balls) enumeration is possible because we set possibilities. In natural cases with unknown frequencies of numerous indistinguishable possibilities, assigning probabilities is often impossible without empirical frequency or justified inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: First instance establishes possibility; subsequent instances establish frequency and control
rubrics_metrics.description: The first observed instance of an event is crucial because it proves the event is possible (shows an adequate cause); subsequent instances indicate the power’s control and invariability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reason straight from one instance to the next without reference to the underlying cause. The first instance changes the epistemic status by introducing the possibility; further instances increase confidence by indexing the cause's steadiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical frequency gives conditional certainty dependent on unchanged collocation of causes
rubrics_metrics.description: If an event never failed in many trials sufficient to eliminate chance, it is empirically certain only so long as the collocation of causes remains the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any inference from past frequency to future probability assumes constancy of relevant causes. If causes change, past frequency may no longer indicate future probability; probability theories cannot overcome unrecognized changes in causal collocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware selection bias and incomplete statement in historical/instance recitals
rubrics_metrics.description: Recitals of instances (especially in economics/politics) are often futile evidence because circumstances are incompletely stated and contrary instances omitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing historical examples or alleged ‘natural experiments’ in social science, demand complete circumstances and beware omitted counterexamples; without this, recitals cannot reliably establish causal claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural experiments imperfect: complex means obscure causal attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural or fortuitous experiments can mimic man-made experiments but often use complex means we cannot analyze; thus they are of little value except to corroborate conclusions derived by other methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: clearing a canopy of clouds affecting dew — we may not know the mechanisms by which cloud-clearing affects deposition, so the natural experiment mainly corroborates already-established conclusions rather than proving new ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalization as heuristic: empirical regularities suggest further inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical generalizations, even if not universally true, can suggest processes of inquiry that lead to discovery of deeper laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empirical regularities (e.g., solubility tendencies) as guides to design investigations aiming to uncover underlying general laws, but treat such generalizations as provisional and potentially remediable by deeper theory.
